primary_meaning: Access, entrance, or passage—most characteristically, access to God, salvation, and eternal life through Christ. A door or gate may therefore represent both the offered way of entry and the decisive boundary between those admitted and those excluded.
primary_basis: John 10:7-9 — Jesus identifies himself as the gate/door through whom one enters and is saved.
Matthew 7:13-14; Luke 13:24 — the narrow gate represents the difficult way leading to life, contrasted with the broad way leading to destruction.
John 14:6 — although not using the door image, it commonly supports the interpretation of Christ as the exclusive way of access to the Father.
Luke 13:25-28; Matthew 25:10-12 — the shut door symbolizes the end of opportunity and exclusion from the kingdom.
Revelation 3:20 — Christ standing at the door and knocking is commonly interpreted as an invitation to fellowship, repentance, or personal reception of Christ.

alternatives.meaning: An opportunity opened by God, especially for ministry, evangelism, or effective service.
Access to heaven, divine revelation, or the presence and purposes of God.
Judgment, exclusion, or the final closing of an opportunity to enter.
Human receptivity or the inward opening of the heart to Christ.
Authority, civic power, security, or vulnerability, reflecting the legal and defensive role of ancient city gates.
The power or domain of death and hostile spiritual forces, especially in the expression “gates of Hades.”

notes: There is broad consensus around the general symbolism of access, entry, and boundary, especially Christ as the entrance to salvation. There is not one fixed meaning for every occurrence: context determines whether the image emphasizes invitation, opportunity, revelation, exclusion, judgment, authority, or security.
